topics: Front matter (PDF pp. 1–6): title leaf and four-page contents; the assigned body comprises Chapters 1–3.
Chapter 1, Fourier Series (printed pp. 1–64; PDF pp. 7–70): periodic signals, harmonic expansions, Hilbert-space structure, applications, and convergence.
1.1 Introduction and Choices to Make (printed p. 1; PDF p. 7): Fourier series as the periodic starting point; passage toward nonperiodic transforms; the spectrum principle.
1.2 Periodic Phenomena (printed pp. 2–3; PDF pp. 8–9): temporal and spatial periodicity, wave frequency and wavelength, crystal lattices, and oriented spatial frequencies.

1.3 Periodicity: Definitions, Examples, and Things to Come (printed pp. 4–8; PDF pp. 10–14): fundamental periods, sums and products of periodic functions, complex exponentials, eigenfunctions, orthogonality, and periodization.
1.4 It All Adds Up (printed p. 9; PDF p. 15): finite harmonic sums and their coefficient extraction.
1.5 Lost at c (printed pp. 10–12; PDF pp. 16–18): complex Fourier coefficients, conjugate symmetry for real signals, average value, and finite Fourier series.

1.6 Period, Frequencies, and Spectrum (printed pp. 13–15; PDF pp. 19–21): harmonic frequencies, spectral line plots, power/energy spectrum, arbitrary-period normalization, and reciprocal period/frequency spacing.

1.7 Two Examples and a Warning (printed pp. 16–20; PDF pp. 22–26): square- and triangle-wave series, infinite high-frequency content caused by jumps and corners, windowing clicks, and instrument timbre.
1.8 The Math, the Majesty, the End (printed pp. 21–25; PDF pp. 27–31): L2 energy and norm, least-squares Fourier approximation, completeness, Parseval/Rayleigh, and Riesz–Fischer.
1.9 Orthogonality (printed pp. 26–32; PDF pp. 32–38): inner products and norms for vectors and functions; orthogonality and orthonormality of complex exponentials.

1.10 Appendix: The Cauchy–Schwarz Inequality and its Consequences (printed pp. 33–35; PDF pp. 39–41): Cauchy–Schwarz, the triangle inequality, integral forms, and existence/bounds for Fourier coefficients.
1.11 Appendix: More on the Complex Inner Product (printed pp. 36–37; PDF pp. 42–43): complex inner products, Hermitian symmetry, and Cauchy–Schwarz in the complex setting.
1.12 Appendix: Best L2 Approximation by Finite Fourier Series (printed p. 38; PDF p. 44): projection proof that Fourier coefficients uniquely minimize mean-square error.
1.13 Fourier Series in Action (printed pp. 39–49; PDF pp. 45–55): heat flow, diffusion, telegraph cables, neutron diffusion, the Dirichlet kernel, impulse trains, and sound synthesis.
1.13.1 Hot enough for ya? (printed pp. 39–47; PDF pp. 45–53): derivation of the heat equation; heat on a circle; seasonal underground temperature; Thomson’s cable law; diffusion case studies.
1.13.2 A nonclassical example: What’s the buzz? (printed pp. 47–49; PDF pp. 53–55): equal-energy harmonic sums, Dirichlet kernels, concentration toward an impulse train, and spectral sound shaping.
1.14 Notes on Convergence of Fourier Series (printed pp. 50–57; PDF pp. 56–63): coefficient decay versus smoothness, uniform convergence for smooth signals, jump values, and Gibbs oscillations.
1.14.1 How big are the Fourier coefficients? (printed pp. 50–52; PDF pp. 56–58): integration-by-parts estimates linking derivative discontinuities to 1/n, 1/n², and higher-order coefficient tails.
1.14.2 Rates of convergence and smoothness (printed pp. 53–54; PDF pp. 59–60): pointwise and uniform convergence with an explicit differentiability-dependent error rate.
1.14.3 Convergence if it’s not continuous? (printed pp. 54–57; PDF pp. 60–63): sawtooth partial sums, midpoint convergence at jumps, and the persistent Gibbs overshoot.
1.15 Appendix: Pointwise Convergence vs. Uniform Convergence (printed p. 58; PDF p. 64): a moving, growing triangular spike that converges pointwise but not uniformly.

1.16 Appendix: Studying Partial Sums via the Dirichlet Kernel: The Buzz Is Back (printed pp. 59–60; PDF pp. 65–66): partial sums as convolution with the Dirichlet kernel and the sine-over-sine closed form.
1.17 Appendix: The Complex Exponentials Are a Basis for L2([0,1]) (printed pp. 61–62; PDF pp. 67–68): three-step density, uniform-convergence, and best-approximation outline for L2 completeness.
1.18 Appendix: More on the Gibbs Phenomenon (printed pp. 62–64; PDF pp. 68–70): Dirichlet-kernel reduction of square-wave overshoot to a sine-integral maximum.
Chapter 2, Fourier Transform (printed pp. 65–94; PDF pp. 71–100): derivation, inversion, transform pairs, duality, symmetry, and shift/scale rules.

2.1 A First Look at the Fourier Transform (printed pp. 65–74; PDF pp. 71–80): periodized rect functions, continuous-spectrum limiting argument, transform and inverse definitions, inversion, bandlimited signals, and Parseval.
2.2 Getting to Know Your Fourier Transform (printed pp. 75–94; PDF pp. 81–100): transform examples and operational rules.
2.2.1 Examples (printed pp. 75–79; PDF pp. 81–85): rect/sinc, triangle/sinc², one-sided exponential decay, Lorentz power profile, and independent-variable scaling.
2.2.2 For Whom the Bell Curve Tolls (printed pp. 79–81; PDF pp. 85–87): Gaussian normalization, self-transform proof, and Euler’s polar-coordinate evaluation of the Gaussian integral.
2.2.3 General Properties and Formulas (printed p. 82; PDF p. 88): transition from a transform-pair storehouse to general operational laws.
2.2.4 Fourier transform pairs and duality (printed pp. 82–85; PDF pp. 88–91): forward/inverse symmetry, reversed signals, transform iteration, and dual pairs sinc/rect and sinc²/triangle.
2.2.5 Even and odd symmetries and the Fourier transform (printed pp. 85–86; PDF pp. 91–92): reversal, conjugate symmetry, and real/imaginary parity consequences.
2.2.6 Linearity (printed p. 86; PDF p. 92): additivity and homogeneity.
2.2.7 The shift theorem (printed pp. 86–87; PDF pp. 92–93): time shifts as unit-magnitude spectral phase ramps.
2.2.8 The stretch (similarity) theorem (printed pp. 87–90; PDF pp. 93–96): reciprocal time/frequency scaling, localization tradeoff, and scaled rect transforms.
2.2.9 Combining shifts and stretches (printed pp. 90–94; PDF pp. 96–100): affine changes, shifted rects, two-sided exponentials, and general Gaussians.
Chapter 3, Convolution (printed pp. 95–136; PDF pp. 101–142): convolution theorem, filtering, differential equations, the central limit theorem, and uncertainty.
3.1 A ∗ is Born (printed pp. 95–98; PDF pp. 101–104): convolution derived from multiplication of Fourier transforms; dual multiplication/convolution rule; rect self-convolution.
3.2 What is Convolution, Really? (printed pp. 99–100; PDF pp. 105–106): LTI context, smoothing/averaging/smearing interpretations, and flip-and-drag visualization.
3.3 Properties of Convolution: It’s a Lot like Multiplication (printed pp. 101–102; PDF pp. 107–108): commutativity, associativity, distributivity, the delta identity foreshadowed, and deconvolution.

3.4 Convolution in Action I: A Little Bit on Filtering (printed pp. 102–106; PDF pp. 108–112): impulse response, transfer function, magnitude/phase effects, and ideal lowpass, bandpass, highpass, and notch filters.

3.5 Convolution in Action II: Differential Equations (printed pp. 106–116; PDF pp. 112–122): derivative theorem; constant-coefficient ODEs; infinite-rod heat kernel; telegraph-cable diffusion; periodic versus infinite heat solutions; Jacobi/Poisson identity.
3.6 Convolution in Action III: The Central Limit Theorem (printed pp. 116–127; PDF pp. 122–133): repeated self-convolution, random variables, densities, moments, independence, and density of sums.
3.7 The Central Limit Theorem: The Bell Curve Tolls for Thee (printed pp. 128–130; PDF pp. 134–136): normalized iid sums, transform-domain proof, and convergence to the standard Gaussian.
3.8 Fourier transform formulas under different normalizations (printed p. 130; PDF p. 136): how transform constants alter inversion, differentiation, and convolution formulas.
3.9 Appendix: The Mean and Standard Deviation for the Sum of Random Variables (printed pp. 131–132; PDF pp. 137–138): convolution derivation of nµ and √nσ scaling.
3.10 More Details on the Central Limit Theorem (printed p. 132; PDF p. 138): control of the Taylor remainder in the characteristic-function argument.
3.11 Appendix: Heisenberg’s Inequality (printed pp. 133–136; PDF pp. 139–142): time/frequency variances, Cauchy–Schwarz proof, Gaussian equality case, and position/momentum interpretation.
key_results: Section 1.1 (printed p. 1; PDF p. 7): the organizing principle is that every signal has a spectrum and is determined by that spectrum; Fourier analysis alternates analysis into frequency components with synthesis back to the signal.
Sections 1.3–1.6 (printed pp. 4–15; PDF pp. 10–21): a period-T signal has harmonics e^{2πint/T} and coefficients c_n=(1/T)∫_0^T f(t)e^{-2πint/T}dt; c_0 is its average value.
Sections 1.5–1.6 (printed pp. 10–15; PDF pp. 16–21): for a real signal, c_{-n}=conj(c_n); |c_n|² is the power/energy spectrum, and the spectral lines n/T are spaced 1/T apart.
Section 1.8 (printed pp. 22–25; PDF pp. 28–31): in L2([0,1]), the degree-N Fourier partial sum is the unique best trigonometric-polynomial approximation in mean-square distance.
Section 1.8 (printed p. 24; PDF p. 30): {e^{2πint}} is an orthonormal basis of L2([0,1]), so Fourier partial sums converge to f in L2.
Section 1.8 (printed pp. 24–25; PDF pp. 30–31): Parseval/Rayleigh identity ∫_0^1|f(t)|²dt=Σ_{n=-∞}^{∞}|f̂(n)|² decomposes signal energy among harmonics.
Section 1.8 (printed p. 24; PDF p. 30): Riesz–Fischer converse—every square-summable coefficient sequence is the Fourier-coefficient sequence of an L2 function.

Section 1.9 (printed pp. 29–32; PDF pp. 35–38): the function inner product (f,g)=∫_0^1 conj(f(t))g(t)dt makes complex exponentials orthonormal; f̂(n) is the projection (e_n,f) in the notes’ slot convention.
Sections 1.10–1.11 (printed pp. 33–37; PDF pp. 39–43): Cauchy–Schwarz |(f,g)|≤||f||||g|| implies the L2 triangle inequality and guarantees bounded Fourier coefficient functionals.

Section 1.12 (printed p. 38; PDF p. 44): the Pythagorean decomposition of approximation error proves equality in the best-approximation bound only when each trial coefficient equals the Fourier coefficient.

Section 1.13.1 (printed pp. 40–43; PDF pp. 46–49): Newton cooling plus conservation yields u_t=kk′u_xx; for u_t=(1/2)u_xx on a unit circle, c_n(t)=f̂(n)e^{-2π²n²t} and u is the periodic convolution of f with Green’s function Σe^{-2π²n²t}e^{2πinx}.
Section 1.13.1 (printed pp. 44–45; PDF pp. 50–51): a sinusoidal annual surface temperature produces u(x,t)=e^{-√(2π)x}sin(2πt-√(2π)x); at √(2π)x=π it is damped to e^{-π}≈0.04 and shifted six months.
Section 1.13.1 (printed pp. 45–46; PDF pp. 51–52): Thomson’s cable model v_t=(1/KC)v_xx gives pulse-peak delay t_max=(1/6)KCx², the law of squares.
Section 1.13.2 (printed pp. 47–50; PDF pp. 53–56): the Dirichlet kernel D_N(t)=Σ_{n=-N}^N e^{2πint} concentrates at integers and tends distributionally toward an integer impulse train.

Section 1.14.1 (printed pp. 50–53; PDF pp. 56–59): integration by parts links regularity to spectral decay—jumps generate O(1/n) coefficients, corners O(1/n²), and jumps in the second derivative O(1/n³), with the pattern continuing.
Section 1.14.2 (printed p. 53; PDF p. 59): if f is p-times continuously differentiable, p≥1, its partial sums converge pointwise and uniformly with max|f-S_N|≤C/N^{p-1/2}.
Section 1.14.3 (printed pp. 56–57; PDF pp. 62–63): for a piecewise C1 periodic signal, S_N(a) tends to half the sum of the left and right limits; at continuity points this is f(a).

Sections 1.14.3 and 1.18 (printed pp. 57, 62–64; PDF pp. 63, 68–70): at a square-wave jump the limiting Gibbs maximum is 1.089490… for a ±1 signal—about 9% overshoot—and the peak narrows but does not disappear.
Section 1.16 (printed pp. 59–60; PDF pp. 65–66): the partial sum is the periodic convolution S_N(t)=∫_0^1D_N(t-s)f(s)ds, with D_N(t)=sin(π(2N+1)t)/sin(πt).

Section 2.1 (printed pp. 68–73; PDF pp. 74–79): letting the period of a periodized finite-duration signal grow and scaling its Fourier coefficients by T yields Ff(s)=∫_{-∞}^{∞}f(t)e^{-2πist}dt and a continuous spectrum.
Section 2.1 (printed pp. 72–73; PDF pp. 78–79): the inverse transform F^{-1}g(t)=∫_{-∞}^{∞}g(s)e^{2πist}ds gives Fourier inversion (f̂)∨=f under suitable hypotheses.
Section 2.1 (printed pp. 73–74; PDF pp. 79–80): a signal is bandlimited when f̂(s)=0 outside a bounded frequency interval; Fourier-transform Parseval is ∫|f(t)|²dt=∫|f̂(s)|²ds.
Sections 2.1 and 2.2.1 (printed pp. 68–77; PDF pp. 74–83): canonical pairs are Π↔sinc and Λ↔sinc², with sinc(s)=sin(πs)/(πs) and Λ=Π∗Π.
Section 2.2.1 (printed pp. 77–78; PDF pp. 83–84): the one-sided decay e^{-at}u(t) transforms to 1/(a+2πis), whose power spectrum 1/(a²+4π²s²) is a Lorentz profile.
Section 2.2.2 (printed pp. 79–81; PDF pp. 85–87): the normalized Gaussian e^{-πx²} is its own Fourier transform; Euler’s double-integral/polar-coordinate argument gives ∫e^{-x²}dx=√π.
Section 2.2.4 (printed pp. 82–85; PDF pp. 88–91): duality and reversal give F²f=f^{-}, F⁴f=f, F(sinc)=Π, and F(sinc²)=Λ.

Section 2.2.5 (printed pp. 85–86; PDF pp. 91–92): Fourier transformation preserves even/odd parity; for real f, f̂(-s)=conj(f̂(s)); real even signals transform to real even functions and real odd signals to purely imaginary odd functions.
Sections 2.2.6–2.2.7 (printed pp. 86–87; PDF pp. 92–93): F is linear, and f(t+b)↔e^{2πisb}F(s), so a time shift changes phase but not spectral magnitude.
Section 2.2.8 (printed pp. 87–90; PDF pp. 93–96): stretch theorem f(at)↔|a|^{-1}F(s/a); squeezing in time stretches in frequency and vice versa.
Sections 2.2.8–2.2.9 (printed pp. 88–94; PDF pp. 94–100): Π_p(t)=Π(t/p)↔p sinc(ps); e^{-a|t|}↔2a/(a²+4π²s²); general shifted/scaled Gaussians remain Gaussian up to phase and reciprocal width.
Section 3.1 (printed pp. 96–98; PDF pp. 102–104): (g∗f)(t)=∫g(t-x)f(x)dx and F(g∗f)=Fg·Ff; dually, F(gf)=Fg∗Ff.

Sections 3.2–3.3 (printed pp. 99–102; PDF pp. 105–108): convolution is commutative, associative, and distributive; when one unit-area kernel is localized near zero it replaces f(t) by a nearby weighted average and typically smooths while spreading support.
Section 3.4 (printed pp. 103–104; PDF pp. 109–110): an LTI convolution filter w=h∗v has W=HV; spectral magnitudes multiply and phases add, so H is the transfer function and h the impulse response.
Section 3.4.1 (printed pp. 104–106; PDF pp. 110–112): ideal lowpass H=Π_{2ν_c} has h(t)=2ν_c sinc(2ν_ct); an ideal bandpass centered at ±ν_0 has b(t)=4ν_c cos(2πν_0t)sinc(2ν_ct).
Section 3.5 (printed p. 107; PDF p. 113): derivative theorem F(f^{(n)})(s)=(2πis)^nFf(s), hence a constant-coefficient differential operator P(d/dx) becomes multiplication by P(2πis).
Section 3.5 (printed p. 107; PDF p. 113): u''-u=-f has solution u=(1/2)e^{-|t|}∗f.
Section 3.5 (printed pp. 108–109; PDF pp. 114–115): for the infinite-rod heat equation u_t=(1/2)u_xx with u(x,0)=f(x), u(x,t)=(2πt)^{-1/2}∫e^{-(x-y)²/(2t)}f(y)dy.

Section 3.5 (printed pp. 114–116; PDF pp. 120–122): periodizing the Gaussian heat kernel gives Σe^{-(x-n)²/(2t)}=√(2πt)Σe^{-2π²n²t}e^{2πinx}; this identifies periodic and infinite-line heat solutions and specializes to Jacobi’s theta identity.
Sections 3.6.5–3.6.6 (printed pp. 124–128; PDF pp. 130–134): the pdf of the sum of independent random variables is the convolution of their pdfs; n iid summands with pdf p have density p^{∗n}.
Sections 3.7 and 3.9 (printed pp. 128–132; PDF pp. 134–138): for S_n=ΣX_k with iid mean µ and standard deviation σ, µ(S_n)=nµ and σ(S_n)=√nσ; (S_n-nµ)/(√nσ) converges in distribution to N(0,1).

Section 3.7 (printed pp. 129–130; PDF pp. 135–136): in the mean-zero, unit-variance case, the normalized density is p_n(x)=√n p^{∗n}(√n x), whose transform [P(s/√n)]^n tends to e^{-2π²s²}, yielding the standard Gaussian.
Section 3.11 (printed pp. 133–135; PDF pp. 139–141): for unit-energy f with centered |f|² and |f̂|², σ(f)σ(f̂)≥1/(4π); equality holds exactly for constant multiples of Gaussians e^{-kx²}.

Section 3.11 (printed pp. 135–136; PDF pp. 141–142): in the quantum interpretation, |ψ(x)|² and |ψ̂(s)|² are position and momentum densities, and noncommuting position/momentum operators prevent simultaneous arbitrary precision.
pedagogy: Osgood develops the subject as a live lecture narrative: he motivates a formula from a concrete problem, derives it in detail, turns it into a definition or theorem, and immediately pressure-tests it on examples. The progression repeatedly crosses among geometric intuition, engineering language, and proof sketches—vector projection motivates L2 Fourier coefficients; increasingly long periodizations motivate the transform; multiplication of transforms motivates convolution; and probability turns repeated convolution into the CLT. Major analytic results are stated precisely but difficult measure-theoretic proofs are openly deferred, while algebraic proofs and transform calculations are worked line by line. Exercises are woven into the prose ('show', 'check', 'match the plots', 'derive this') and presume single- and multivariable calculus, complex numbers, differential equations, and some linear algebra; probability is introduced from scratch in Chapter 3. Warnings about normalization, variables, conjugation, and unjustified integrals are a recurring metacognitive device. Applications—music, heat flow, telegraphy, filters, statistics, and quantum mechanics—are used as structural explanations rather than afterthoughts.

gems: Section 1.1 (printed p. 1; PDF p. 7): the course’s compact north star—every signal has a spectrum and is determined by it—sets up analysis and synthesis as the two directions of the subject.

Section 1.2 (printed pp. 3–4; PDF pp. 9–10): blue and yellow stripe fields appear greenish when spatial frequency is high, turning Fourier resolution into a perceptual experiment and raising a hysteresis/orientation question.
Section 1.6 (printed pp. 15–16; PDF pp. 21–22): 'larger period in time, smaller spacing of the spectrum' is an aphorism that anticipates both the transform limit and time/frequency reciprocity.

Section 1.7 (printed pp. 16–20; PDF pp. 22–26): square waves need arbitrarily high frequencies because finite sinusoid sums are continuous; triangle corners still force infinite terms because finite sums are smooth. Sharp window cuts therefore produce audible clicks.

Sections 1.7–1.8 (printed pp. 20–21; PDF pp. 26–27): bassoon and flute spectra explain different timbre on the same note, while the oboe’s unusually rich harmonics make it useful for orchestral tuning because every instrument can find something of itself in the oboe.

Section 1.8 (printed p. 26; PDF p. 32): the John Tukey paraphrase—one would not want to fly in a plane whose design depended on Riemann versus Lebesgue integrability—deflates a difficult analytic caveat without hiding it.

Section 1.9 (printed pp. 26–27; PDF pp. 32–33): Osgood’s practical Pythagorean-theorem story lays out a rectangular field by checking a diagonal, then transfers that geometric orthogonality intuition to functions.

Section 1.13.1 (printed p. 45; PDF p. 51): underground seasonal temperature at the depth √(2π)x=π has only e^{-π}≈4% amplitude and is six months out of phase—mathematical proof of why a cellar stays steady and reverses the seasons.

Section 1.13.1 (printed pp. 45–47; PDF pp. 51–53): Thomson’s 1855 law of squares says 1,000 cable miles impose 100 times the delay of 100 miles, not 10. The first Atlantic cable ignored the model, used too much voltage, and failed after three weeks: 'They fried it.'

Section 1.13.1 (printed p. 47; PDF p. 53): neutron-diffusion models gave about 60 kg of U-235 in a 9 cm radius sphere, versus 200 kg from a cruder model; the discrepancy becomes a high-stakes lesson in model accuracy.

Section 1.13.2 (printed pp. 47–50; PDF pp. 53–56): summing every harmonic with equal energy creates the 'continuous-time buzz'; its Dirichlet-kernel peaks tend toward an impulse train, bridging sound synthesis and sampling.

Section 1.14.3 (printed pp. 56–57; PDF pp. 62–63): Michelson and Stratton’s mechanical Fourier-series drawing machine produced jump ripples they blamed on machinery; Gibbs showed the fixed ~9% overshoot was mathematics, not a broken device.
Section 1.18 (printed pp. 62–64; PDF pp. 68–70): the universal Gibbs peak emerges from (2/π)∫_0^π(sin s)/s ds and sits at t=1/(2N+1), a crisp endpoint for the Dirichlet-kernel story.
Section 2.1 (printed p. 69; PDF p. 75): after deriving rect↔sinc from ever-longer periodizations, Osgood remarks that many electrical engineers see sinc in their dreams.

Section 2.1 (printed p. 70; PDF p. 76): two actual Fry’s Electronics installations embody Fourier waveforms in a storefront and a mechanical sculpture—an unexpected pause between the rect example and the general transform limit.

Section 2.2.2 (printed pp. 80–81; PDF pp. 86–87): Euler’s famous Gaussian-integral trick squares an impossible one-dimensional integral, changes to polar coordinates, and makes the extra Jacobian factor r solve it exactly.

Section 2.2.4 (printed pp. 84–85; PDF pp. 90–91): the identity F²f=f reversed, hence F⁴=I, makes Fourier transformation a four-step cycle; Osgood notes that some people attach mystical significance to it.
Section 3.2 (printed pp. 99–100; PDF pp. 105–106): 'Convolution is what convolution does' rejects a single metaphor, then offers the more useful trio: weighted averaging, smoothing, and smearing.
Section 3.2.1 (printed p. 100; PDF p. 106): Π is discontinuous but Π∗Π=Λ is continuous; one self-convolution removes jumps while leaving corners, a minimal worked demonstration of smoothing.
Section 3.3 (printed p. 102; PDF p. 108): deconvolution appears as spectral division Fh/Fg, and zeros of Fg expose why separating a signal from noise is ill-conditioned rather than merely algebraic.

Section 3.4.1 (printed pp. 104–106; PDF pp. 110–112): an ideal sharp lowpass needs an infinite sinc impulse response and cannot be achieved exactly; highpass and notch responses remain inaccessible at this stage until delta functions arrive.

Section 3.5 (printed p. 107; PDF p. 113): a second-order ODE u''-u=-f collapses to multiplication in frequency and returns as convolution with (1/2)e^{-|t|}, putting the earlier two-sided exponential pair to work.

Section 3.5 (printed pp. 114–116; PDF pp. 120–122): a single Gaussian identity makes heat flow on a circle and on an infinite rod literally the same solution after periodization, and its x=0 special case is Jacobi’s theta identity.

Section 3.6 (printed pp. 116–118; PDF pp. 122–124): repeated convolution turns both a rectangle and a literally random jagged signal into a Gaussian-looking curve—'from seeming chaos'—before probability explains why.
Section 3.6.1 (printed p. 118; PDF p. 124): 'A random variable is a number you don’t know yet' is the deliberately informal definition that opens the probability interlude.

Section 3.6.6 (printed pp. 124–125; PDF pp. 130–131): one fair die is a six-bin rect; two dice yield a triangular distribution with six of 36 ways to make seven, so probability convolution becomes countable and visible.

Sections 3.6–3.7 (printed pp. 118, 128–130; PDF pp. 124, 134–136): the Lippmann quip—experimenters trust the normal approximation as a theorem, mathematicians as experiment—frames the CLT proof via [P(s/√n)]^n→e^{-2π²s²}.

Section 3.11 (printed pp. 133–135; PDF pp. 139–141): the time/frequency uncertainty lower bound is proved with Parseval, Cauchy–Schwarz, and one integration-by-parts trick; equality selects Gaussians yet again.

Section 3.11 (printed pp. 135–136; PDF pp. 141–142): position is multiplication by x, momentum is (1/2πi)d/dx, and their noncommutation converts the analytic variance bound into quantum measurement uncertainty.
